name: The Degsnė Forest Larch
species: European Larch, Polish larch variety (Larix decidua var. polonica)

location.address: Degsnė Forest, Balbieriškis forestry district, Nemuno Loops Regional Park, Prienai District, Lithuania; via a gravel forest road off the Kaunas-Alytus road (route 130), about 3km north of Balbieriškis / 7km south of Prienai
location.neighbourhood: Degsnė Forest, Nemuno Loops Regional Park

access: Free, public state forest within Nemuno Loops Regional Park. Reached by a good-quality gravel forest road, about 2.5-3km off route 130 (Kaunas-Alytus), turning off shortly before the Balbieriškis outcrop (Balbieriškio atodanga). No gate or permission needed.
transport: No public transport reaches the forest road itself; nearest towns are Balbieriškis (about 3km) and Prienai (about 7km). A car or bicycle is the practical way in.
verify_notes: RECORD CLAIM, clears the single-tree destination bar: this is documented as the tallest tree growing in Lithuania, 49.0m (height to first green branches 29.0m), part of the Degsnė larch stand (Degsnės maumedynas) which is itself Lithuania's tallest forest (average height ~42m). Two independent sources agree: lt.wikipedia's dedicated article (Degsnės miško maumedis) and saugoma.lt, the Lithuanian State Protected Areas Service's own register entry, titled explicitly 'aukščiausias Lietuvos medis' (Lithuania's tallest tree). A third source, the Prienai tourism site infoprienai.lt, runs a page with the same title and confirms the directions. Girth 186cm at 1.3m (slender for the age, typical of larch, a fast vertical grower rather than a thickener). AGE: the larch stand was planted in 1849 ('pirmieji maumedukai... buvo pasodinti', per saugoma.lt), which is a documented planting date for this specific stand rather than a bridge claim from an unrelated garden; lt.wikipedia's figure of 150 years, given at the tree's 2002 designation, is consistent with an 1849 planting (2002-1849=153). Protected since 1960 (forest stand) / designated as an individual botanical natural heritage object in 2002. Condition noted 'satisfactory' with some overmaturity and fungal signs at the 2002 survey; no more recent vitality report found this pass, but tourism sites (infoprienai.lt, naturama.lt, pacukelias.lt) all describe it in the present tense as a current attraction, and it remains a live listed destination. Photos on Commons (Degsnės_maumedis.JPG, Degsnės_maumedis,_kamienas.JPG) show a living, foliage-bearing conifer with a documented trunk. No legend found beyond the record claim itself; none needed given the record.

name: The Great Thuja of Kintai

location.address: Beside the historic Kintai Forestry Office building, Uosto g. 10, Kintai, Šilutė District, Nemuno Delta Regional Park, Lithuania

access: Free and genuinely public. Two routes are both described: a marked ~1km forest trail from Kintai Middle School's car park, or the Kintai Forestry Office's own recreational trail; the tree stands in an open meadow beside the forestry building, within Nemuno Delta Regional Park.
transport: No direct public transport to the trailhead; Kintai village itself is reached by regional bus from Šilutė (about 15km) or Klaipėda. Walk in from the village.
verify_notes: RECORD CLAIM, clears the single-tree destination bar: documented as the tallest/largest giant arborvitae (Thuja plicata, a North American species, in cultivation in Europe since 1863) in Lithuania, and per lt.wikipedia 'manoma, jog Europoje aukstesne didzioji tuja auga tik Sveicarijoje' (believed the only taller one in Europe grows in Switzerland) -- this specific superlative is sourced but hedged as belief/reputation rather than a measured European survey, so state it as reported rather than certain. Four independent sources agree closely (lt.wikipedia, zpasaulis.lt, checkinlithuania.com, siluteinfo.lt, the Silute tourism authority's own English page). CONTINUED GROWTH IS THE ALIVE-NOW EVIDENCE: height measured 1973 (~16m, girth 85cm), 2004 (18.2m, diameter 1.02m = girth ~320cm), 2012 and again 2021 (both 19.5m) -- a nearly 50-year measurement series showing the tree actively growing into the 2020s, about as strong a vitality record as this project ever gets. Two-stemmed, so ring count is not possible; multiple sources independently hedge the planting date as 'not known precisely' but 'presumed' to coincide with the neighbouring Kintai Forestry Office building's construction, 1902-1912 -- this is the classic bridge-claim shape (a nearby building's date standing in for the tree's own), so age_estimate is kept broad and flagged rather than stated as fact; no source ties the tree to the building's construction directly, only proximity and folk presumption. Designated a nature monument in 1986 and a nationally significant protected object in 1987. Girth recorded as the 2004 diameter (1.02m) converted via pi to 320cm; a more recent girth figure was not found alongside the 2021 height reading.
